A workable white body. Shapes and fires like clay, but comes out of the kiln bright white instead of terracotta.
Fired hotter and cleaner than earthenware, so it takes the metals a ceramic crucible cannot - gold, silver, brass, copper and aluminium. Iron and steel are still the ceramic one's job.
Holding molten metal. Keep filling it, then pour it into an ingot mold at the furnace.
Shaped porcelain, still soft. Fire it before it is any use.
Fired far hotter than earthenware. It will not crack when you pour.
Porcelain, shaped but not yet fired. Brittle until it sees a kiln.
Finely ground china. Mixed with water and a little clay it makes porcelain slip.
Sharp white fragments. Grind them into porcelain powder.
Bind a ceramic spearhead to a shaft using ties, strips, twine, or tape.
Cast slip into a plaster mold to form an unfired piece.
Build a wooden frame for making plaster molds around a modeling-clay master.
Pour full crucibles into an ingot mold. The mold is kept.
Cast grogged slip into a plaster mold to form a hollow unfired piece. Same result as plain slip, slightly more Pottery XP.
Cast regular slip into a plaster mold to form a hollow unfired piece.
Break a chunk of china down into shards.
Tip the soil back out. The pot is left clean.
A pot needs soil in it before anything will grow.
Fire the piece in a kiln to harden it. Takes a fire source and a log or charcoal, like any kiln firing.
The glaze melts to a glass skin. A glazed jar seals like a canning jar.
Needs a kiln, something to light it, and fuel.
A long, hot firing. Porcelain needs it.
Fire the crucible in a kiln. Needs fuel and something to light it.
A long, hot firing. Porcelain needs it.
Brush glaze onto an unfired jar. Fired, it comes out watertight and safe to preserve food in.
Grind shards into a fine white powder.
Grind ceramic shards into fine powder using a mortar and pestle.
Stir ceramic powder into a bucket holding at least 10 L of water. The same bucket ends up holding 10 L of grog slurry.

Take a bucket holding 5 L of clay slip and stir in 5 L of grog slurry from any container. The slip bucket ends up holding 10 L of grogged slip. Pour off any slip above 5 L first - whatever is left in the bucket is thrown out with the mix.
Knapp ceramic shards into a usable tool or weapon part using a hammer.
Knead modeling clay back into regular clay.
Slip and quicklime, mixed thin in a bowl. Quicklime is what makes it melt to glass.
Work 0.25 L of grogged slip into a binder - beeswax (from HydeCo. Bees), a bag of sand or a bag of dirt - to make modeling clay.
Paint a fired ceramic piece with a paintbrush and one dab from a can of paint. The can you use sets the colour.
Repaint the coat of a painted ceramic gnome with one dab of paint. The hat keeps its colour - the crafting preview always shows a red hat, but your gnome keeps its own.
Paint the deer with a paintbrush and dabs of paint.
Paint a fired ceramic egg with a paintbrush and one dab from a can of paint - the can sets the colour. Patterned eggs (speckled, striped, zigzag, squiggle, squiggle-and-dot) also take a dab of white.
Paint the frog in its natural colours with a paintbrush and a dab each of green, black and white paint. It becomes a Ceramic Pot Scrubber Frog.
Paint the jack o' lantern with a paintbrush and dabs of paint.
Any paint works, and the pot can be repainted as often as you like.
Repaint the stem of a painted ceramic mushroom with one dab of paint. The cap keeps its colour - the crafting preview always shows a red cap, but your mushroom keeps its own.
Throw a plant pot on the wheel. It still needs firing.
Make a plaster mold from a modeling-clay master using a casting frame.
Stiffens porcelain slip into a workable body. Beeswax, sand or dirt all bind it.
Mixed in the bucket you are holding. Fills it with ten litres of porcelain slip; anything already in the bucket is poured out first.
Move the plant into a pot of your own. It keeps growing; only the pot changes.
Shape a modeling-clay piece with a clay tool. Figurines become the master for a plaster mold; other pieces go straight to the kiln.
Shape the white body on a pottery surface. It fires white, so there is nothing to paint.
Press porcelain into a bar mold.
Throw a crucible from porcelain clay. It has to be fired before it will hold anything molten.
Press porcelain into an ingot mold.
Stir clay into a bucket holding at least 8 L of water. The same bucket ends up holding 10 L of clay slip; pour it out and it is a plain bucket again.
Break a finished ceramic piece back into shards.
Break a finished porcelain piece back into shards.
Melt scrap down into a porcelain crucible at a furnace. Keep adding until it is full, then cast it.
Lift the plant out with its root ball. You get the pot back with its soil.
Squash an unfired piece back into clay. Only works before it goes in the kiln - once fired, smash it for shards instead.
Smash a ceramic item into shards.
A spear with a ceramic tip.
Needs %1 more and an empty wooden pallet.
You made a living at the wheel and the kiln. Pottery comes much faster, you keep your tools in better shape, and you already have an artisan's eye for clay and glass.
